[[File:Octahemioctahedron.stl|thumb|3D model of an octahemioctahedron]]

In [[geometry]], the '''octahemioctahedron''' or '''octatetrahedron'''{{sfnp|Coxeter|Longuet-Higgins|Miller|1954|p=417}} is a [[nonconvex uniform polyhedron]], indexed as {{math|U{{sub|3}}}}. It contains twelve faces (eight [[Triangle|triangles]] and four [[Hexagon|hexagons]]), twenty-four edges, and twelve vertices. Its [[vertex figure]] is an [[antiparallelogram]]. Since its hexagonal faces pass through its center, it is a [[hemipolyhedron]].

== Construction and properties ==
An octahemioctahedron can be constructed from four diagonals of a cube that bisect the interior into four hexagons, and the edges form the structure of a [[cuboctahedron]]. The four hexagonal planes form a polyhedral surface when eight triangles are added. Thus, the resulting polyhedron has 12 faces, 24 edges, and 12 vertices. If six squares replace the triangular faces, the resulting polyhedron becomes a [[cubohemioctahedron]].{{r|ps}} The octahemioctahedron is a [[uniform polyhedron]], with the [[vertex figure]] being an [[antiparallelogram]].{{r|clm}}

It is the only hemipolyhedron that is [[orientable]], and the only uniform polyhedron with an [[Euler characteristic]] of zero, a topological [[torus]].{{sfnp|Coxeter|Longuet-Higgins|Miller|1954|p=417}}

The octahemioctahedron belongs to a family of concave [[antiprism]]s "of the second sort".{{r|opm}}

== Octahemioctacron ==
[[File:Hexahemioctacron.png|thumb|The dual of an octahemioctahedron]]
The dual of the octahemioctahedron is the '''octahemioctacron''', with its four [[Vertex (geometry)|vertices]] at infinity. Since the hemipolyhedra have faces passing through the center, the dual figures have corresponding [[Vertex (geometry)|vertices]] at infinity; properly, on the [[real projective plane]] at infinity. {{harvtxt|Wenninger|2003}} stated that they are represented with intersecting [[prism (geometry)|prisms]], each extending in both directions to the same vertex at infinity, in order to maintain symmetry. In practice, the model prisms are cut off at a certain point that is convenient for the maker. Wenninger suggested these figures are members of a new class of [[stellation]] figures, called ''stellation to infinity''. However, Wenninger also suggested that strictly speaking, they are not polyhedra because their construction does not conform to the usual definitions.{{r|wenninger}}
